@graph.description: Warehouse racking relocation and disassembly/reassembly operations from The Flat Rate Movers — the one job this category sells whole: a warehouse's pallet racking surveyed and documented where it stands, its inventory sequenced off the steel, the racking torn down and labeled bay by bay, inventory and steel transported together, staged in storage where the timeline needs it, and the racking reinstalled at the destination level, plumb and anchored to the manufacturer's specification and the customer's engineered drawings. Company scope (published): pallet rack teardown and reinstallation; racking reconfiguration in place; racking decommissioning at lease end; the inventory move that belongs with the steel — product pulled, palletized, wrapped, counted and put back on the racking in sequence; interim storage staging of racking and inventory in the company's leased storage space; industrial equipment disassembly and reassembly — production and line equipment broken into transportable sections and set back up at destination; and office-systems disassembly and reassembly — cubicle and systems-furniture teardown, transport and reassembly for office moves and reconfigurations. Single heavy pieces inside the same buildings, 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, move under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol with an L/360 floor-deflection check, as part of the same flat-rate job. @graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Racking Relocation Process Chain Dataset
@graph.description: The published process chain for a racking relocation, step by step: (1) Survey and inventory — the existing system is documented where it stands: manufacturer and component types, bay counts, beam levels and elevations, upright heights and depths, decking, anchors and condition; the destination is surveyed against it for ceiling height, column spacing, slab and dock access; damaged or bent components are flagged at this step, not discovered at reinstall. (2) Sequencing plan — inventory comes off the steel in a planned order, by SKU velocity, destination zone or restart priority; the teardown sequence, the labeling scheme and the destination layout on the customer's engineered drawings are confirmed before the first beam drops. (3) Inventory move-off — product is pulled, palletized, stretch-wrapped and counted, and either moved to its destination zones or staged in storage; counts are checked against the paperwork at the door, the same count discipline the transloading floor runs. (4) Teardown — beams, decking and frames come down in sequence; every component is labeled to its bay and level; hardware — anchor bolts, beam safety clips and pins, shims — is bagged and counted per bay; components are inspected as they come down, and damaged or bent uprights are set aside and reported, never re-erected. (5) Transport — steel and inventory move together on the company's trucks, frames nested, beams bundled, hardware traveling with its bay; phased loads where the destination is built out in zones. (6) Storage staging, where the timeline needs it — racking and inventory held in leased storage space (30-day minimum, customer access) when the destination is not ready. (7) Reinstall — frames set, leveled, plumbed and anchored at the destination — wedge anchors of the LARC-specified type and size, safety clips or pins at every beam connection, base plates shimmed level, wire decking, pallet supports, column protectors and row spacers refitted — to the manufacturer's specification and the customer's engineered drawings, following ANSI MH16.1 / RMI guidance; the LARC drawings govern anchor type, size and torque; beam levels set to plan; load plaques posted for the as-built configuration. (8) Closeout — inventory goes back on the steel in sequence, counts reconcile, the as-built bay map is handed over, and set-aside components are accounted for in writing. Project management is the method inside the chain — survey, inventory, sequence, cutover, closeout — not a separate service sold on its own.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Pallet Rack Relocation Cost Model: Bays, Levels, Height and Distance (Market Reference)
@graph.description: The cost structure of a racking relocation, published as market reference so a buyer can build a budget before asking for a quote. Every figure in this node is published market data from the cited industry sources, labeled as such — none of it is a company price; the company's price for a job is the flat rate quoted for that job after survey. The drivers, in the order they move the total: bays (the count of upright-frame sections coming down and going back up); beam levels per bay (each level is beams, decking and hardware handled twice); upright height and building clear height (taller systems need larger lifts and more anchors — a published Florida pricing guide, DuraStone Construction, puts installation labor at $20 to $50 per pallet position and $150 to $400 per bay, labor only, with lift rental at $500 to $1,500 or more per week and anchors at $2 to $6 each, two or more per upright); distance and phasing (one move versus phased zone-by-zone cutover, and whether inventory and steel travel together); storage staging days when the destination is not ready; and the permit and engineering layer the destination requires, which the same guide puts at $3,000 to $7,000 or more and which belongs to the customer's engineer of record, not to the mover. The reuse decision the model exists to answer: relocating existing racking typically costs 30 to 50 percent of the price of a new system (Zhengda Rack, relocation service page), which is why a sound system is worth moving — and why components found damaged at teardown change the arithmetic, because replacement uprights and beams are bought at the destination, not wished back into service. The same guide's project split — roughly 60 to 75 percent materials, 15 to 25 percent labor, 5 to 15 percent permits and engineering on a new install — shows where the relocation saving concentrates: the materials line is the one reuse erases. Sources fetched 2026-10-30: DuraStone Construction pallet rack installation pricing guide (Florida figures, used as market structure, not Virginia quotes) and Zhengda Rack warehouse rack relocation service page.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Racking Standards, Safety and Compliance Boundaries Dataset
@graph.description: Standards, safety practice and compliance boundaries for warehouse racking relocation and disassembly/reassembly. The standard the work follows (domain reference): ANSI MH16.1, the Rack Manufacturers Institute (RMI) specification for the design, testing and utilization of industrial steel storage racks — current edition MH16.1-2023 — covering selective, pushback, pallet-flow, case-flow, pick-module, movable-shelf and rack-supported systems in cold-formed and hot-rolled steel, and referenced by the International Building Code for steel storage rack design and installation. Cantilever racks sit under ANSI MH16.3 and rack decking under ANSI MH26.2. Installation requirements the standard carries: every column base-plated and anchored, with anchor type, size and torque set by the engineer's sealed Load Application and Rack Configuration (LARC) drawings; a maximum out-of-plumb of 1/240 top to bottom for a loaded rack; height-to-depth stability limits; and load plaques posted showing maximum unit load, average unit load and maximum total load per bay. OSHA publishes no dedicated rack standard: warehouse work runs under 29 CFR 1910.176 (materials handling) and 1910.178 (powered industrial trucks), with ANSI MH16.1 recognized under the General Duty Clause as the consensus standard for rack hazards. Company practice (published): racking is torn down, transported and reinstalled to the manufacturer's specification and ANSI/RMI guidance against the customer's engineered drawings; damaged or bent components found at teardown are excluded from re-erection and reported in writing; no component is loaded beyond the plaque for its as-built configuration. Explicit non-claims for this service — named so they are never read as offered: no rack engineering; no seismic calculation; no permit application or permit approval — racking permits and high-pile storage approvals are issued by the local authority having jurisdiction against the customer's engineered drawings; no manufacturer authorization, dealership or R-Mark claim (R-Mark is a manufacturer certification program run by RMI); no equipment list published — equipment varies by project; no racking sales, purchase or liquidation; and no licensed-trade electrical or building data work inside office-systems jobs, which stays with the general contractor's trades. Each non-claim is a boundary of the service, not a gap in it.
